third_paragraph.2: Rossel and colleagues quantified the interception response of fish to dislodged flies, and Gerullis and Schuster quantified jet control at controlled target heights, so each behavior is measured in its own preparation.

3.add: Sampling every 20 ms resolves the position and heading of the fish across the whole response.

4.add: Under these conditions the landing point is fixed by release height and initial horizontal velocity, the two variables a fish needs to combine.

5.add: The turn must therefore depend on the angle between the current orientation of the fish and the direction of the predicted landing point.

6.add: Aiming at the future water-entry point and not at the current prey position is the defining feature of a predictive start.

7.add: The early motion therefore sets the turn and acceleration, and visual corrections enter only after the initial phase.

8.add: The input to this relation is height, speed and direction, and the output is the landing point, so the horizontal screen supplies the inputs without the fall.

9.add: Stage one rotates the body toward the chosen destination, and stage two completes the turn while the fish accelerates.

10.add: Peak values of 4500°/s and 2.1 m/s define the performance range that any controlling circuit must produce.

11.add: The difference between the two behaviors lies in how the turn angle is chosen: away from a threat for an escape, toward a predicted catch point for a predictive start.

third_paragraph.12: Turns from 4° to 156° are produced by scaling the first-stage bend, which gives the fish a continuous range of headings from one motor pattern. Any adequate mechanism must allow rapid movement with continuously variable turning and speed.

13.add: The nearly fixed mouth-tip position means that changes in the jet reflect the control of the shot by the fish.

14.add: A fish aiming at 60 cm therefore completes focusing farther along the path than a fish aiming at 20 cm.

15.add: Longer-range shots need a jet that stays intact over a greater distance, and the reduced shaft modulation fits that requirement.

third_paragraph.16: The data support adjustable velocity gradients and reject an ordinary rigid-projectile description of the jet. Faster water emitted behind slower water catches the tip, which is how a velocity gradient gathers the water toward the impact point.

17.add: Stable jets therefore depend on additional controlled variables, such as the timing of water release at the mouth.

third_paragraph.18: Fluid properties identical to control water and displacement below 0.26 mm point to the time-varying mouth opening as the adjustable element. Water composition and whole-body motion do not supply the range adjustment.

19.add: Releasing water for a longer interval supplies the faster subsequent water that long-range jets require.

20.add: The up-forward region therefore provides the finest anatomical sampling along the direction in which the fish aims.

21.add: Regional sensitivity can shape which contrasts are available against an aerial background. Spectral sensitivity and the spatial resolving power measured anatomically are distinct constraints on visual aiming.

22.add: Expressing velocities as those of an object about 30 cm from the eye relates the electrode responses to the speeds of real moving targets.

23.add: A decoder that reconstructs velocity from absolute latencies indicates that the timing of spikes across the population carries velocity information within tens of milliseconds of movement onset.

24.add: A spike count over 100 ms is slow relative to a predictive response, whereas relative first-spike latency stays near 10 ms across velocities.

25.add: Combining cells improves the estimate because their timing patterns carry complementary information about velocity.

26.add: Each tectal neuron is thus described by where in space and when in time a stimulus changes its firing.

third_paragraph.27: Excitatory and inhibitory filters describe how earlier light levels increase or decrease the response of a cell. The analysis adds information missed by an average alone, because it captures several filters per cell.

28.add: The diverse combinations provide candidate transformations of visual timing before a motor decision.

third_paragraph.29: The atlas also maps catecholaminergic and cholinergic markers, which identify cell groups by the transmitter they use. A cholinergic neuron uses acetylcholine.

30.add: Antidromic stimulation travels backward from axon toward cell body, so the recorded all-or-none signal reports the spike of the cell itself.

31.add: The archerfish cell therefore has the same overall plan as the goldfish cell, with dendrites receiving input and the axon hillock initiating the spike.

32.add: Two crossed giants of about 71.9 µm in diameter mean that each Mauthner cell sends a fast signal to the opposite side of the spinal cord.

33.add: A spike onset latency of 0.265 ms and a half-maximal duration of 0.54 ms mark a rapidly conducting, fast-signaling output neuron.

third_paragraph.34: Latency and amplitude measure different properties of an input, so an earlier onset is separate from the size of the influence on firing. Acoustic PSPs mean that the Mauthner cell receives mechanosensory input as well as visual input.

35.add: Larger but delayed visual input fits a pathway with more processing stages before the Mauthner cell.

third_paragraph.36: Passive decay with distance means that a signal arriving far from the soma shrinks before it reaches the spike-initiation region, so the amplitude gradient indicates where an input entered.

37.add: Recovery with a fast and a slow component limits how quickly the cell can fire a second spike.

third_paragraph.38: The reduction of an antidromic spike during a PSP measures a functional inhibitory effect. Matching time courses in the two species make a shared inhibitory network the parsimonious explanation.

39.add: Declining errors over successive shots show that the fish recalibrate the shot using the outcome of earlier shots.

40.add: Aftereffects that decline over several shots show the compensation being unlearned as the original conditions return.

third_paragraph.41: An egocentric adjustment ties the correction to the direction the fish is facing. The compensation therefore follows the body-relative relation and not the fixed airflow direction in the tank.

42.add: The learned deflection of 39.8° became part of the mapping from early motion to destination.

43.add: The tests used heights for which competing accounts predicted different destinations, so the initial turn identifies which relation the fish applied.

44.add: The same early motion thus leads to different destinations depending on the object that the fish sees.

45.add: A rule can therefore be selected on the fly, without advance preparation, within a start that begins in under 100 ms.

inserts.title: A predictive start is aimed at the future landing point
paragraphs: A predictive start is a rapid turn and acceleration that sends a fish toward the point where prey will land, begun while the prey is still in the air. It differs from pursuit, in which the fish follows the current position of a visible target.

Rossel and colleagues recorded fish and dislodged flies from above. Responding fish initiated a rapid turn within approximately 100 ms, aligned toward the future landing point, and accelerated along that heading while the prey remained airborne.

Securing the food requires reaching the water-entry point before another fish does, so the turn must be aimed at a destination that the prey has not yet reached. The shooter and nearby bystanders can both respond.
notes: A predictive start is the central behavior of this lecture.
Definition.
It is a rapid turn and acceleration toward the point where prey will land.
It begins while the prey is still falling.
Contrast with pursuit.
Pursuit follows the current position of a visible target.
A predictive start aims at a destination that does not yet contain the prey.
The recordings.
Rossel and colleagues filmed fish and dislodged flies from above.
Responding fish turned within approximately 100 ms.
Heading and acceleration.
The turn aligned the body toward the future landing point.
The fish then accelerated along that heading while the prey remained airborne.
Competition.
The fish that shoots and nearby bystanders can both respond.
Reaching the water-entry point first secures the food.
Two motor demands.
Shooting requires control of a water jet, and interception requires a fast turn and acceleration.
Gerullis and Schuster recorded shots at target heights of 20, 40 and 60 cm.
Consequence.
The motor command must specify a destination from early information about the prey.

inserts.title: Heading is the direction of the body axis
paragraphs: Heading is the direction in which the body axis points at a given moment. A bystander's initial heading can differ greatly from the direction in which a dislodged fly moves, so the angle of the required turn varies from trial to trial.

Rossel and colleagues sampled this angular relation at both 20- and 40-cm prey heights, including orientations that required large turns before acceleration toward the destination. The fish occupied different positions and orientations in the tank.

The turn needed to reach the destination depends on the heading at the moment of the response. A fixed turn angle cannot succeed from every starting orientation, so the responder must convert prey-motion information into a turn measured from its own body axis.
notes: Heading is the reference for measuring every turn in these experiments.
Definition.
Heading is the direction in which the body axis points.
It is measured at the moment the response begins.
Variation.
A bystander can face almost any direction relative to the fly.
The angle of the required turn therefore changes from trial to trial.
Sampling.
Rossel and colleagues sampled the angular relation at 20- and 40-cm prey heights.
Some orientations required large turns before acceleration.
Positions in the tank.
Responders occupied different positions as well as different orientations.
Turning generally ended before the prey entered the water.
Body-centered turn.
The fish must express the destination as a turn from its own body axis.
Consequence for models.
A fixed turn angle cannot explain interception.
The responder must transform prey-motion information into a turn requirement.
Links to the data.
The angular relation was sampled at both prey heights.
Orientations that needed large turns were included, which covers the range of initial headings.

inserts.title: Open-loop control runs without feedback
paragraphs: Open-loop control is a mode in which a movement is set in advance and runs without adjustment from feedback about its own outcome. Closed-loop control compares the outcome with the goal during the movement and corrects it.

Rossel and colleagues tethered prey with a thin filament. The fly moved freely for slightly more than 100 ms, then stopped and reversed when the filament became taut. Fish still turned and initially accelerated toward the landing point predicted from the early motion.

The initial turn and acceleration behaved as an open-loop command, because the contradicting trajectory did not alter them at once. Corrections appeared much afterward, so visual feedback acts on the response only after the initial phase.
notes: The tether experiment separates a preset command from continuous tracking.
Open loop.
A movement runs as set in advance.
Feedback about its outcome does not adjust it.
Closed loop.
The outcome is compared with the goal during the movement.
Errors are corrected as they appear.
The manipulation.
Rossel and colleagues tethered prey with a thin filament.
The fly moved freely for slightly more than 100 ms before the filament became taut.
Prey behavior.
The fly stopped and reversed its direction.
The visible trajectory then contradicted the early motion.
Fish response.
Fish still turned and accelerated toward the landing point predicted from the early motion.
Corrections appeared much afterward.
Meaning.
The first phase of the response was set by early motion information.
Visual feedback adjusts the response only after the initial commitment.
Timing.
The early free motion lasted slightly more than 100 ms.
The reversal therefore began after the fish had the information needed to choose a turn.

inserts.title: A virtual landing point is defined by starting conditions
paragraphs: A virtual landing point is the destination at which prey with a given initial height and horizontal velocity would have entered the water if it had been allowed to fall. The experimenter defines it from the starting conditions, because the prey on the screen never descends.

Rossel and colleagues placed prey on a transparent horizontal glass screen at 20 or 40 cm height. Air from a blast pipe moved the object horizontally at speeds within the natural take-off range, so the target moved without descending toward the water.

Errors relative to the virtual point were centered near zero at both heights, so fish turned toward the destination that the motion would have produced. The response therefore depends on initial height, speed and direction, and not on a visible water-entry event.
notes: The virtual landing point allows the experimenter to test prediction without a fall.
Definition.
It is the destination where prey with a given height and horizontal velocity would have entered the water.
The prey on the screen never reaches the water.
The screen.
Prey sat on a transparent horizontal glass screen at 20 or 40 cm height.
Air from a blast pipe moved the object horizontally.
Speeds.
The speeds were within the natural take-off range.
The target moved without descending toward the water.
Fish response.
Fish turned toward the virtual landing point.
Errors relative to this point were centered near zero at both heights.
Extrapolation.
Straight extrapolation of the actual horizontal path gives no finite water-entry point.
The fish must use another relation.
Consequence.
The relation is built from initial height, speed and direction.
A visible water-entry event is not required.
Controls the variables.
Height was set at 20 or 40 cm.
Horizontal speed was set by the air flow.

inserts.title: Angular speed and linear speed measure different things
paragraphs: Angular speed is the rate at which the body axis rotates, expressed in degrees per second. Linear speed is the rate at which the center of mass moves through the water, in meters per second, and acceleration is the rate at which either speed changes.

Wöhl and Schuster reconstructed angular and linear motion from high-speed video. Predictive starts reached angular speeds above 4500°/s and linear speeds as high as 2.1 m/s, with peak linear acceleration reaching 120 m/s².

Angular speed generally peaked during initial bending, whereas the strongest linear speed occurred after straightening began. These different time courses separate reorientation from acceleration toward the predicted destination, so one maneuver sets both heading and take-off speed.
notes: Two kinds of speed describe the same fast start.
Angular speed.
It is the rate of rotation of the body axis in degrees per second.
It measures how fast the fish turns.
Linear speed.
It is the rate at which the center of mass moves through the water.
It measures how fast the fish travels toward the prey.
Acceleration.
Acceleration is the rate at which either speed changes.
Peak linear acceleration reached 120 meters per second squared.
Values.
Angular speeds exceeded 4500 degrees per second.
Linear speeds reached 2.1 meters per second.
Timing.
Angular speed generally peaked during initial bending.
The strongest linear speed occurred after straightening began.
Method.
Wöhl and Schuster reconstructed the motion from high-speed video.
Position records were smoothed before differentiation.
Consequence.
The same maneuver can set both heading and take-off speed.
Peak acceleration.
Peak linear acceleration reached 120 meters per second squared.
The values come from demanding interception responses.

inserts.title: A focused jet gathers water into a compact tip
paragraphs: A focused jet is one in which the water has gathered into a concentrated tip, so that the water arrives at the target as a compact mass. The focusing distance is the distance along the path at which the water finishes gathering.

In shots aimed at a target 60 cm high, the water had not finished assembling at the jet tip after 30 cm of travel, and near impact the tip became concentrated. A shot aimed at 20 cm was already focused at that closer target height.

Preimpact tips were similarly concentrated across the three target heights, whereas intermediate shapes differed with the intended range. The focusing distance is therefore adjusted to the distance of the target and is not fixed near the mouth.
notes: Focusing describes how the water of a shot is arranged as it travels.
Definition.
A focused jet has gathered its water into a concentrated tip.
The focusing distance is where this gathering finishes.
Long-range shot.
For a target 60 cm high, the water had not finished assembling after 30 cm.
The tip became concentrated near impact.
Short-range shot.
A shot aimed at 20 cm was already focused at that closer height.
Image comparison.
Gerullis and Schuster compared original high-speed images at equivalent travel positions.
They also compared the preimpact phase.
Preimpact tips.
They were similarly concentrated across the three target heights.
Intermediate shapes differed with the intended range.
Consequence.
A fixed-distance account would have the water assemble near the mouth.
The data instead show that focusing distance follows the target distance.
Comparison of heights.
The 20 cm shot and the 60 cm shot differ in where the tip finishes forming.
The impact shape is similar in both.

inserts.title: A velocity gradient speeds rear water catch the tip
paragraphs: A velocity gradient is a difference in speed between parts of the same moving body of water, here between the water emitted first at the front and the water emitted behind it. Faster rear water can catch up with slower front water.

Gerullis and Schuster measured the tip speed during the first 20 ms of jet formation. The tip accelerated even while the jet rose against gravity, because it remained connected to subsequently emitted water moving faster than the early water.

Published fits gave total speed increments of 2.7–3.8 m/s, and the increment increased with target height. A larger difference between early and subsequent water therefore belongs to a longer intended range, unlike an ordinary rigid projectile.
notes: The jet is a stream of water emitted over time, and its speed varies along its length.
Definition.
A velocity gradient is a difference in speed along the moving water.
Here the rear water moves faster than the front water.
Tip acceleration.
The tip accelerated during the first 20 ms of formation.
It did so even while the jet rose against gravity.
Cause.
The tip stayed connected to subsequently emitted water.
That water moved faster than the early water.
Fitted values.
Limiting speeds were 5.8–6.8 meters per second.
Total speed increments were 2.7–3.8 meters per second.
Time constants.
Fitted time constants ranged from 6.6 to 20.0 ms.
Range dependence.
The speed increment increased with target height.
A longer range is linked to a larger early-to-late velocity difference.
Contrast.
An ordinary rigid projectile does not have such a gradient.
Link to the mouth.
The velocity difference between early and subsequent water depends on how the mouth releases the water.
The gradient is therefore a product of the control of the shot by the fish.

inserts.title: Resolving power is the finest detail an eye can sample
paragraphs: Resolving power is the finest spatial detail an eye can distinguish, expressed in cycles per degree. A cycle is one bright–dark repetition in a spatial pattern, and more cycles per degree indicate finer sampling by cones and ganglion cells.

Temple and colleagues mapped cones and retinal ganglion cells in _Toxotes chatareus_. The highest cone densities exceeded 50,000 cells/mm², and ganglion-cell density approached a one-to-one relation with cone density there. Anatomically estimated resolving power reached 6.9 cycles/degree, compared with 2.2 cycles/degree along the downward axis.

A ventral high-density region aligns with the up-forward visual direction used during spitting. Sampling is therefore finest where the fish aims and coarser elsewhere, instead of equal across the entire visual field.
notes: Resolving power links retinal anatomy to the direction of aiming.
Definition.
Resolving power is the finest spatial detail an eye can distinguish.
It is expressed in cycles per degree.
Cycle.
A cycle is one bright–dark repetition in a spatial pattern.
More cycles per degree mean finer sampling.
Cone density.
The highest cone densities exceeded 50,000 cells per square millimeter.
Ganglion-cell density approached a one-to-one relation with cone density there.
Estimates.
Resolving power reached 6.9 cycles per degree in the ventral region.
It was 2.2 cycles per degree along the downward visual axis.
Alignment.
The high-density region faces the up-forward direction used during spitting.
Methods.
Temple and colleagues used retinal preparations and anatomical counts in Toxotes chatareus.
Consequence.
The retina samples most finely along the aiming direction instead of equally across the field.
Directions in the visual field.
The up-forward direction is the one used during spitting.
The downward axis has lower resolving power.

inserts.title: A multielectrode array records many retinal neurons
paragraphs: A multielectrode array is a grid of recording electrodes on which an isolated tissue is placed, so that the spikes of many neurons are recorded at the same time. Retinal ganglion cells are the output neurons of the retina, and their spikes carry visual information to the brain.

Kretschmer and colleagues placed isolated archerfish retinas on the array and projected alternating black and white bars. The grating stayed present while movement began at randomly selected velocities, and the 400-µm bars moved upward or downward.

Recorded ganglion cells produced sharply timed responses after movement onset. Because the grating was already present, the responses reflect the onset of motion and not the sudden appearance of a new object.
notes: The array records the retinal output directly.
Definition.
A multielectrode array is a grid of recording electrodes under an isolated tissue.
It records the spikes of many neurons at the same time.
Ganglion cells.
They are the output neurons of the retina.
Their spikes carry visual information toward the brain.
Stimulus.
Alternating black and white bars were projected onto the retina.
The bars were 400 micrometers wide.
Motion onset.
The grating stayed present while movement began.
Starting velocities were chosen at random.
Direction.
Bars moved upward or downward.
Movement history varied so that direction reversal did not occur in every step.
Response.
Ganglion cells produced sharply timed responses after movement onset.
Meaning.
The responses reflect motion onset and not the sudden appearance of an object.
Velocity scale.
Velocities are expressed as those of an external object about 30 cm from the eye.
They are not speeds across the retinal surface.
Randomization.
Starting velocities were chosen at random, so the responses cannot be explained by a fixed order of stimuli.

inserts.title: Relative latency uses an internal timing reference
paragraphs: Relative latency is the time of a cell's first spike measured from the onset of the population response and not from the stimulus clock. Absolute latency, by contrast, is measured from the moment the experimenter presents the stimulus. Both are first-spike measures, and they differ only in their reference.

Kretschmer and colleagues compared absolute latency with first interspike interval, spike rate over 100 ms, and latency relative to population response onset. The first interval and the tested rate measure reconstructed velocity poorly.

Relative first-spike latency performed better, although its median stayed near 10 ms across velocities, because the pattern across cells kept the velocity information. It uses an internal reference and does not need the experimenter's stimulus clock.
notes: Relative timing solves the problem of an unknown stimulus onset.
Absolute latency.
It is measured from the moment the stimulus is presented.
The experimenter knows this moment, but the brain has to infer it.
Relative latency.
It is measured from the onset of the population response.
The reference comes from the cells themselves.
Comparison.
Kretschmer and colleagues also tested the first interspike interval.
They tested a spike rate over 100 ms as well.
Rate measures.
The first interval and the tested rate reconstructed velocity poorly.
Result.
Relative first-spike latency performed better.
Its median stayed near 10 ms across velocities.
Why it works.
The pattern across different cells kept the velocity information.
Single medians did not carry it.
Timescale.
A 100 ms spike count is slow compared with a predictive response.
Population view.
Each cell supplies a different tuning profile.
The pattern of relative timing across cells carries the velocity.
Reference.
The population response onset serves as an internal clock that the retina itself provides.
Absolute latency needs the stimulus clock of the experimenter.

inserts.title: A spike-triggered average describes preferred stimuli
paragraphs: A spike-triggered average is the mean of the stimulus patterns that preceded each spike of a neuron. It describes which stimulus features, in space and time, tend to make the neuron fire.

Reichenthal and colleagues recorded extracellular activity in the optic tectum of archerfish while presenting random checkerboards. About 68% of the sampled cells had a monophasic temporal profile, whereas the remaining group had two phases with opposite contrast signs. Mean estimated response latencies were 54.5 ms and 60 ms for these groups.
Receptive fields ranged from nearly circular to elongated. The average therefore gives a spatial pattern and a temporal profile for each cell, which is the information used to compare tectal neurons.
notes: The spike-triggered average turns a spike record into a description of the preferred stimulus.
Definition.
It is the mean of the stimulus patterns that preceded each spike.
It reveals which features make a neuron fire.
Stimulus.
Random checkerboards were presented to the archerfish.
Extracellular activity was recorded in the optic tectum.
Receptive fields.
A receptive field is the stimulus region and pattern that changes a neuron's activity.
Fields ranged from nearly circular to elongated.
Temporal profiles.
About 68% of sampled cells had a monophasic profile.
The remaining cells had two phases with opposite contrast signs.
Latencies.
Mean estimated latencies were 54.5 ms and 60 ms for the two groups.
Structure.
The tectum is a midbrain structure that receives visual input.
It takes part in sensorimotor processing.
Consequence.
Each cell is described by where and when a stimulus changes its firing.
Nonlinear step.
An average alone can miss part of the response structure of a cell.
Additional analyses use several temporal filters per cell.

inserts.title: Antidromic stimulation identifies a cell by its axon
paragraphs: Antidromic stimulation sends a spike backward along an axon, from the axon toward the cell body, so that the neuron fires without synaptic input. A field potential is the extracellular voltage generated by the currents of a cell or group of cells. The signal can therefore be used to locate the cell before it is filled with dye.

Machnik and colleagues stimulated the spinal cord and searched the archerfish hindbrain for a characteristic short-latency, all-or-none extracellular field potential. Increasing a stimulus above threshold changed whether the signal occurred but did not progressively scale its amplitude.

Each side of the hindbrain contained a distinct focus, consistent with a paired neuronal source. Intracellular penetration and subsequent staining then linked that source to a cell with Mauthner-like morphology.
notes: Antidromic stimulation makes it possible to find a specific neuron without knowing its inputs.
Definition.
A spike is sent backward along the axon toward the cell body.
The neuron fires without synaptic input.
Field potential.
It is the extracellular voltage produced by the currents of a cell or group of cells.
Search.
Machnik and colleagues stimulated the spinal cord.
They searched the hindbrain for a short-latency, all-or-none potential.
All or none.
A stimulus above threshold changed whether the signal occurred.
The amplitude did not scale with stimulus strength.
Paired source.
Each side of the hindbrain contained a distinct focus.
Identification.
Intracellular penetration and staining linked the source to a cell.
The cell had Mauthner-like morphology.
Summary.
The electrical signature allows the cell to be found by its response and not by its size.
Staining then confirms its shape.
Threshold behavior.
Raising the stimulus above threshold switched the signal on and did not make it larger.
This all-or-none property is what a spike of a single large cell would produce.

inserts.title: A length constant measures passive decay
paragraphs: A length constant describes the distance over which passive voltage spread along a dendrite is attenuated. A short length constant means that a signal fades quickly with distance from the place where it entered. Distance along the dendrite is the variable that these recordings sample.

Machnik and colleagues recorded at different positions along the Mauthner lateral dendrite and corrected the signals for the nearby extracellular field. Reconstructed spike amplitude decayed passively with length constants of 141–164 µm in the tested cells.

Acoustic PSPs were larger at a distal lateral-dendrite position than close to the soma, whereas visual PSPs decreased toward the distal dendrite. The opposite gradients place the entry sites of the two inputs at different dendritic locations.
inserts.citation: Machnik et al. (2018b); Machnik et al. (2018a)
notes: Passive decay allows amplitude at a recording site to report where an input entered.
Definition.
A length constant is the distance over which passive voltage spread is attenuated.
A short value means a signal fades quickly.
Recordings.
Machnik and colleagues recorded at several positions along the lateral dendrite.
They corrected the signals for the nearby extracellular field.
Values.
Reconstructed spike amplitude decayed with length constants of 141–164 micrometers.
Acoustic input.
Acoustic PSPs were larger at a distal lateral-dendrite position than near the soma.
This fits input arriving laterally.
Visual input.
Visual PSPs showed the opposite gradient.
Their amplitude decreased toward the distal dendrite.
Consequence.
The two senses enter the cell at different dendritic locations.
Link to the circuit.
Both input types are recorded in the same identified cell.
Their different entry sites show that the pathways reach separate dendritic regions.
Correction for the field.
Recorded signals were corrected for the extracellular field near the cell.
Without the correction the spike amplitude would be misjudged.

inserts.title: An aftereffect reveals retained compensation
paragraphs: An aftereffect is an error in the direction opposite to the original disturbance that appears when the disturbance is removed. It indicates that the movement had been recalibrated to the disturbance and is a standard signature of motor adaptation. The term applies to the first shots after the airflow stops.

Volotsky and colleagues compared baseline shots, a perturbation period of horizontal airflow, and shots after airflow removal. After the perturbation ended, errors appeared in the opposite direction and declined over several subsequent shots.

A compensation learned during the perturbation therefore initially persisted when the physical deflection was removed. If each shot only corrected the visible outcome afterward, removal of the disturbance would not produce this systematic initial bias.
notes: The washout phase tests whether a correction was learned.
Definition.
An aftereffect is an error opposite to the original disturbance.
It appears when the disturbance is removed.
Sequence.
Volotsky and colleagues compared baseline shots, a perturbation period and shots after airflow removal.
Perturbation.
Horizontal airflow deflected the jet.
Errors increased at first and then declined over successive shots.
Washout.
After the airflow ended, errors appeared in the opposite direction.
They declined over several subsequent shots.
Interpretation.
The compensation learned during the perturbation persisted at first.
The shot had been recalibrated.
Control logic.
A fish that only corrected the visible outcome would show no systematic opposite bias.
Motor adaptation predicts it.
Baseline to washout.
Baseline shots define the normal accuracy of the fish.
The sequence from baseline through perturbation to washout separates recalibration from simple correction.
Airflow direction.
Trials in both airflow directions tested whether adjustment was limited to one direction of deflection.
The target itself did not move.
